title: 45. Award Talk: Investigating the impacts of gestational management on ewe lamb reproductive dynamics.
content:
Abstract
Extensively managed ewes are often grazed through winter while gestating, requiring strategic management and supplementation to meet nutritional requirements supporting maternal maintenance and fetal growth. Due to seasonal declines in forage quantity and quality, ewes may experience nutrient challenge outside traditional supplementation periods. Maternal nutrition during gestation programs offspring development with lasting implications for productivity and reproductive efficiency, dependent on the timing, duration, and severity of insult. Thus, the objective of this project was to determine the long-term impacts of divergent gestational environments on growth performance and reproductive tissue development. Ewe lambs were produced from dams fed either a balanced diet formulated to meet requirements for the entirety of gestation (CON; n = 18) or a high-fiber diet simulating winter forage conditions in the Intermountain West from 30-125 days of gestation (NC; n = 12). Post-weaning, offspring were transitioned to a diet formulated to meet growth requirements for puberty attainment in the first year. Beginning at approximately 6 months of age, ewe lambs were bled twice weekly for puberty determination via serum progesterone concentration. Upon puberty attainment, lambs were estrus synchronized and harvested, followed by tissue specific analysis of reproductive organs via histology and RT-PCR. NC lambs tended (P < 0.10) to attain puberty later than CON lambs. At harvest, age adjusted body weight, hot carcass weight, and uterine weight were lighter (P < 0.05) in NC lambs compared to CON, while ovary weight did not differ. Caruncle counts were similar between groups; however, the ratio of caruncle count:uterine weight tended (P < 0.10) to be greater in NC lambs compared to CON. Additionally, uterine luminal fluid glucose concentrations tended (P < 0.10) to be greater in NC lambs compared to CON. There were no differences in follicle classification counts or total follicle numbers. Transcript abundance for PCNA, AMH, Erα, and Erβ, did not differ between groups. Relative protein abundance for Erα and Erβ was reduced (P < 0.05) in NC lambs compared to CON, while PCNA and AMH did not differ. Reductions in relative protein abundance despite similar gene expression suggest post-transcriptional regulation or altered translational efficiency. Given that these receptors mediate estrogen-dependent regulation of folliculogenesis and uterine development, reduced receptor abundance may impair tissue responsiveness to endocrine signaling and contribute to animal variation. Alterations in caruncle density relative to uterine weight and luminal glucose concentrations further suggest modified uterine structural and metabolic dynamics in NC offspring. Collectively, these findings indicate that poor maternal nutrition during gestation induces persistent alterations in reproductive dynamics, potentially delaying reproductive maturity and reducing functional reproductive efficiency in replacement ewe lambs.
